research_concepts: predictive relationship between reorganization and PPP change
methodological_questions: How to measure offensive reorganization relative to a baseline L
Whether reorganization magnitude during absence spells predicts change in team points per possession
How to control for confounding by opponent defensive strength and simultaneous roster changes
Power and minimum detectable effect size given limited number of absence spells (n≈148)
Reliability of derived play-type possession metrics for short absence spells

historical_evidence.finding: Connector absence displaces team offensive identity (D_A) more than usage-matched non-organizer absence. Unmatched conn vs role D_A 0.2020 vs 0.1021, t=5.97 p=2.87e-08. Usage-matched vs role: paired dD_A +0.1151, P(conn>ctrl)=81.2%, t=6.35 p=7.35e-09 n=96. Vs terminal: +0.0777 t=2.37 p=0.0261 n=25.

A possession's ending state changes opponent points/possessions in the next 90-180s. 90s vs MADE_DEAD: TURNOVER_LIVE dOppPts=+0.510 dNetPts=-0.306 (dOppPPP=+0.055, dOppPoss=+0.298); MISSED_DEAD dNetPts=-0.112; PUTBACK dNetPts=+0.078. Volume, not PPP, carries most of the live-TO cost.
Putback suppression apparent effect on next possession vanishes after matching on game state; raw effect was a score/context confound.
Apparent next-game playing-time response to opponent 3P luck (G_opp3 +0.0625 SE 0.0180) disappears when controlling for game-N role (+0.0020 SE 0.0178), revealing a confound artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Causal isolation of putback suppression on next possession without adequate control for score/state confounds
failed_approaches.why: Confounding by game state (score, margin) produced a spurious effect that collapsed after matching; labeled artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attributing next-game playing-time changes to opponent 3P luck without controlling for the player's game-N role
failed_approaches.why: Confounding by game-N share; effect disappeared after including that control, establishing artifact.

evidence_establishes: Connector absences produce a larger break in offensive identity (D_A) than usage-matched non-organizer absences, confirming that absence type influences reorganization magnitude.
Prior artifact cases (SF-APPS-041, SF35) demonstrate that apparent relationships in basketball data often vanish once confounds like game state or player role are properly controlled.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the amount of offensive reorganization predicts the change in points per possession; no prior study tested this predictive link.
The expected effect size or direction of any relationship between reorganization and PPP change.
The reliability and stability of the reorganization metric across different absence spell lengths and contexts.
own_inferences: The research question is novel in the context of this project's prior work: the predictive component has not been addressed.

The available data (n≈148 absence spells) and the inherent noisiness of both reorganization and PPP metrics likely yield low power, making a definitive test unlikely to produce a clear supported/rejected outcome.
Even if a statistical association were found, confounding by opponent defensive strength, simultaneous injuries, and schedule could produce spurious correlations, as seen in SF-APPS-041 and SF35.
Without a validated reorganization metric and careful handling of baseline (L) and measurement error, any test risks being an artifact.
A well-controlled regression with team/season fixed effects and opponent adjustments would be the minimum viable design, but it is still severely underpowered with current data.
uncertainties: The exact operational definition of L and the reorganization metric (how much the offense reorganizes relative to L) has not been specified or validated.
The possession count per absence spell and the resulting reliability of both reorganization and PPP change measures are unknown but likely low for short spells.
No prior estimate exists for the correlation between reorganization and PPP change, making power calculations speculative.
Spell selection criteria (minimum games, possessions) will further reduce the effective sample size below 148.
The partial 2025-26 data may introduce further noise or incomplete spells.

historical_effect.explanation: No prior decision existed. The historical evidence directly informed the assessment: FAM:SF-APPS-088 shows that reorganization can be measured and varies by absence type, while SF-APPS-041 and SF35 illustrate the serious risk of confounding artifacts. This reinforced the caution against proceeding without addressing low power and confounders, but did not change a pre-existing decision.

blocking_constraints.text: Only ~148 absence spells are available, many of short duration, yielding low power to detect a modest correlation between noisy measures. After requiring minimum possessions, effective sample size will shrink further.

The relationship between reorganization and PPP change is highly susceptible to confounding by opponent defensive strength, home/away, rest, and other roster changes; prior artifact cases (SF-APPS-041, SF35) underscore this risk.

The reorganization metric derived from play-type distributions likely has low reliability for short spells, and PPP change is notoriously noisy; measurement error will attenuate any true signal and inflate required sample size.
Absences often follow extreme offensive performance; regression to the mean could create a spurious correlation between apparent reorganization and PPP change if not properly controlled.

prior_work.summary: FAM:SF-APPS-088 established that connector absences cause larger offensive identity breaks (reorganization) than usage-matched non-organizer absences, but did not test whether reorganization predicts changes in points per possession. No prior work has examined this predictive relationship.

risks.text: Insufficient number of absence spells (n≈148, reduced after quality filters) to reliably detect a plausible effect size against measurement noise.
Opponent strength, schedule, and simultaneous roster changes may drive both perceived reorganization and PPP changes, creating spurious associations.
Both the reorganization metric (derived from play-type distributions) and PPP change are measured with substantial error, especially for short absence spells.
Absences often follow extreme periods; without careful baseline adjustment, regression to the mean may masquerade as a reorganization-PPP relationship.
Many absence spells have too few possessions to estimate the reorganization metric reliably, forcing either exclusion or low-quality measurements.
If the baseline L uses information from the absence period or post-absence, the reorganization measure may be contaminated by outcomes.

design.estimand: Linear regression slope of the change in team offensive rating (points per 100 possessions) from the pre-absence baseline to the absence period on a continuous measure of offensive reorganization (e.g., divergence of play-type frequencies from the pre-absence L, computed over the first 5 games of the absence).
design.unit: Absence spell (a specific player's continuous missed games).
design.sample: All absence spells of at least 3 games and with at least 100 offensive possessions in both the pre-absence window (last 10 team games before absence) and the absence window, from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons.
design.power: For n=148 spells, power to detect a correlation of 0.20 is approximately 0.66 at α=0.05 two-sided; after correcting for measurement error, likely below 0.50. With additional future seasons (~250 spells) power could reach 0.80 for r=0.20.
design.controls: Team fixed effects, season fixed effects, opponent adjusted offensive rating (10-game rolling average), home/away indicator, days of rest, number of other missing rotation players, and pre-absence team offensive rating (to account for regression to the mean).
design.falsification: Test that the same reorganization measure does not predict change in team defensive rating (points allowed per 100 possessions). A null result on defense would support specificity.
design.multiplicity: Single primary hypothesis; no additional hypothesis tests beyond the falsification check, so no multiplicity adjustment required.
design.decision_rule: Reject null of zero slope if p < 0.05 (two-sided) with cluster-robust standard errors by team. Otherwise report the effect size with 95% confidence interval and declare the result inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season per-game play-by-play, substitution rotation, and derived play-type possession records, as of 2026-11-01.

methodological_questions: measuring offensive reorganization relative to baseline
predicting change in points per possession from reorganization
power and effect size for predicting PPP change
distinguishing absence effect from other lineup changes
args.query: Does the degree of offensive reorganization during a player's absence predict the change in team points per possession?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 4 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
How much the offense reorganizes (relative to L) predicts the change in points per possession.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=986; n=148, mde rho; 148 spells

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["player absence", "offensive reorganization", "points per possession", "offensive efficiency", "L metric"], "methodological_questions": ["measuring offensive reorganization relative to baseline", "predicting change in points per possession from reorganization", "confounding by opponent defensive strength", "sample size for absence spells", "power and effect size for predicting PPP change", "distinguishing absence effect from other lineup changes"], "query": "Does the degree of offensive reorganization during a player's absence predict the change in team points per possession?"}}

reasoning_details.text: We are in Stage 1, so I need to identify research concepts and methodological questions, then call retrieve_history. Let's parse the research question: "How much the offense reorganizes (relative to L) predicts the change in points per possession." This seems to be about player absence and offensive reorganization. "Relative to L" - L might be a metric, perhaps "L" is a team's offensive organization metric? Could be "Lineup" or something? Not sure, but the concepts include offensive reorganization, player absence, points per possession change. Also "reorganizes (relative to L)" likely means reorganization relative to some baseline (maybe "L" is League average or a specific metric). I'll need to query history. Let's think about research concepts: player absence, offensive reorganization, points per possession. Methodological questions: measuring reorganization, predicting change in offensive efficiency, potential confounders (e.g., opponent defense, lineup changes), sample size, sparsity of absence spells. I'll construct query: "How does offensive reorganization during player absence predict change in points per possession?" Research concepts could be: "player absence impact on offense", "offensive reorganization metric", "points per possession prediction". Methodological questions: "measuring offensive reorganization", "causal effect of absence on offensive efficiency", "confounding by opponent quality", "sample size and power". I'll retrieve_history with these.

We are in stage 2 after the retrieval. The retrieved records include four study families: FAM:SF-APPS-088, FAM:SF-APPS-078, FAM:SF-APPS-041, FAM:SF35. Let's analyze each to see how they relate to the research question: "How much the offense reorganizes (relative to L) predicts the change in points per possession." We need to summarize historical evidence, what it establishes and doesn't, assess testability, identify risks, make a decision and design.

First, understand the question: It's about player absence and offensive reorganization. The variable "L" likely is a baseline level of offensive organization (maybe from the glossary). The research question asks: how much the offense reorganizes relative to L (i.e., the degree of offensive reorganization during a player's absence, presumably compared to some baseline) predicts the change in points per possession. So we have two variables: a measure of reorganization (relative to L), and change in PPP (points per possession). The prediction relationship: reorganization predicts the change in PPP. So it's a correlation/regression type question: Does the magnitude of reorganization during an absence spell predict how much the team's offensive efficiency (PPP) changes?

Now, look at the retrieved records:

FAM:SF-APPS-088: "Offensive-identity resilience: connector absence vs usage-matched others". It found that connector absence displaces team offensive identity (D_A) more than usage-matched non-organizer absence. The result includes D_A measurements. This seems relevant: it deals with offensive identity displacement during absence. D_A might be a measure of offensive reorganization. The question is whether reorganization predicts change in PPP. This study shows that connector absence causes larger identity breaks. But does it relate reorganization to PPP change? The record doesn't mention PPP explicitly. It mentions D_positive as no failure, positive result. It has risks: MECHANICAL_FLOOR, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER. It mentions a comparison of D_A between groups. So it doesn't directly test the predictive relationship between reorganization and PPP change. It might have measured D_A and perhaps PPP change separately, but the study's hypothesis was only about D_A differences between absence types. Could be related but not answering the current question. So we can note that prior work has identified that connector absence causes larger offensive identity breaks (reorganization), but hasn't tested whether that reorganization predicts PPP change.

FAM:SF-APPS-078: "Channel 2: possession ending state vs next 90-180s volume/points". This is about how possession ending state (e.g., turnover live, made dead) affects opponent points/possessions in next 90-180s. Not directly about absence and reorganization. But it might relate to PPP changes due to certain events. Not very relevant.

FAM:SF-APPS-041: "PUTBACK suppression matched-pair isolation (star vs team)". This is an artifact study: putback suppression effect disappeared after matching, was a score/context confound. Shows the risk of confounding and the need for careful matching. Could be relevant as a warning about confounds in similar analyses. It's a failed approach in that an initial finding was an artifact. So we can include it in failed_approaches as a caution.

FAM:SF35: "Next-game playing-time response to opponent 3P luck (carryover)". This is also an artifact: an apparent effect (opponent 3P luck influencing next-game playing time) disappeared after controlling for game role. Again, demonstrates confounding risk. The failure mechanism is artifact (C_artifact). So both of these can be used as failed approaches illustrating the need for robust controls and confound handling.

Thus, the historical evidence directly relevant to the question is limited. There's no study that directly tested whether reorganization predicts PPP change during absence. FAM:SF-APPS-088 is the closest: it studied offensive reorganization (D_A) but only compared absence types, not predicting PPP change. So prior work partly answered parts (connector absence causes larger reorganization), but the predictive link to PPP change is not established. We can use FAM:SF-APPS-088 as evidence that reorganization can be measured and differs by absence type. But the question asks whether that reorganization predicts PPP change. That's unknown.

Now, we need to assess testability. The question: "How much the offense reorganizes (relative to L) predicts the change in points per possession." This implies we have a continuous measure of reorganization (amount of reorganizing) and a continuous outcome: change in PPP. Probably we would look at absence spells: during a player's absence, measure the degree to which the offense's play-type distribution or other identity shifts from the baseline (L). L could be the pre-absence offensive identity (play-type frequencies, etc.) based on glossary. Then we measure the change in the team's offensive efficiency (PPP) during the absence relative to before (or compared to expected). Then we regress change in PPP on reorganization measure. So it's a correlational design.

Potential issues: 
- Measuring reorganization: need a robust metric. The D_A from FAM:SF-APPS-088 might be that metric. But is it already defined? In the data description, we have "derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database". So reorganization could be measured as divergence of play-type distribution between the pre-absence period and the absence period. That's plausible.
- Change in PPP: need to account for opponent defensive strength, home/away, other lineup changes, etc. PPP is noisy and has a low signal-to-noise ratio, so many observations might be needed to detect an effect.
- Sample size: "Units available: n=986; n=148, mde rho; 148 spells". This suggests there are 986 something (maybe player-seasons?), 148 spells? Let's interpret: n=986 might be total something, n=148 might be number of absence spells, mde rho possibly the minimum detectable effect correlation. So only 148 absence spells available. That is relatively small for detecting a modest correlation between two continuous variables, both measured with noise. So SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER risk.
- Confounding: teams may change other things during absence (e.g., opponent adjustments, injuries to multiple players, schedule). The reorganization measure itself may be influenced by opponent defensive schemes. For example, a team facing tough defenses might look more disorganized, and also have lower PPP. So spurious correlation. Need to control for opponent defensive rating, game location, rest days, other injured players, etc.
- Reverse causality or mechanical relationship: The reorganization measure might be partly driven by PPP change (if the offense is less efficient, maybe they change plays). But the question is predictive, so time ordering could be established if we measure reorganization early in the absence spell and later PPP change, but still could be confounded.
- LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD: if the metric uses information from the absence period to define baseline, but careful definition could avoid that.
- RTM_SELECTION: Absences might occur after unusual performance; regression to the mean could cause both apparent reorganization and PPP change.
- MEASURE_RELIABILITY: How reliable is the reorganization metric? It might be based on limited possessions.
- EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: some absence spells are short (one game), so possession counts may be small, leading to unreliable measures.

Thus, testability: it's possible but challenging. I'd assign a probability of testable, say 0.6, because the data exist and metrics can be derived, but power might be low and confounding may prevent clear inference. The design would need to carefully control for confounders and have enough spells.

Now, prior work: already_answered? No, the retrieved records haven't answered this predictive question. So "partly" because they measured reorganization but not the prediction. Cited: FAM:SF-APPS-088.

Historical evidence: list each record with status and finding. For FAM:SF-APPS-088: status is "supported"? auto_outcome_status is "supported". Finding: Connector absence displaces team offensive identity (D_A) more than usage-matched non-organizer absence. That's about reorganization, not PPP change. For the others: FAM:SF-APPS-078 is "not a hypothesis test", descriptive. FAM:SF-APPS-041: "artifact". FAM:SF35: "artifact". So we'll list all four.

Failed approaches: FAM:SF-APPS-041: what failed: attempting to isolate causal effect of putback on next possession without adequately controlling for game state; artifact due to confounding. FAM:SF35: what failed: attributing next-game playing time response to opponent 3P luck without controlling for role; artifact. These are general lessons: need to control for confounders and avoid spurious correlations.

Evidence establishes: that absence type (connector vs other) affects the degree of offensive reorganization (D_A). That reorganization can be measured. That prior studies have identified confounding as a major threat (putback, 3P luck) leading to artifacts.

Evidence does not establish: whether the amount of reorganization predicts the change in PPP, nor the magnitude of any such relationship.

Own inferences: The research question is novel in the context of this project's prior work. The data should allow construction of reorganization and PPP change variables. However, the limited number of absence spells (148) and potential noise may yield insufficient power to detect a realistic effect size. Moreover, confounding by opponent strength and simultaneous team changes may bias estimates. A carefully controlled regression with appropriate fixed effects and sensitivity analyses might be possible, but the risk of null or inconclusive result is high.

Uncertainties: The exact definition of L and reorganization metric; the reliability of derived play-type possession records; the distribution of spell lengths; the actual effective sample size after excluding spells with too few possessions; the expected effect size (no prior estimate for correlation between reorganization and PPP change). Also, the data version may be partial for 2025-26 season, but the study could use earlier seasons.

Now, decision: I lean towards do_not_proceed because the main risk is low power and confounding, and the question might be untestable with only 148 spells. But the instruction says: even if do_not_proceed, describe the minimum viable test. Possibly proceed_with_changes: gather more data (future seasons) or pool with other leagues? But as given, we can only decide based on available data. I'll say do_not_proceed given the small sample and high risk of confounding leading to unreliable inference. But I'll outline a design that would be needed if proceeding.

Design: The estimand: the linear relationship between offensive reorganization (measured as divergence of play-type frequencies from pre-absence baseline L to the first N games of absence) and the change in team offensive rating (points per 100 possessions) from pre-absence to absence period, controlling for opponent defensive strength, game location, rest, and other injuries. Unit: absence spell (each player absence episode). Sample: 148 spells from 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons, excluding spells shorter than 3 games or with less than 100 possessions. Power: Assuming a correlation of 0.2, with 148 spells power is about 0.66 at alpha 0.05; but after accounting for measurement error, power lower. Controls: fixed effects for team and season, opponent adjusted offensive rating using rolling average, indicator for home games, days since last game, number of other missing players. Falsification: test that reorganization does not predict change in defensive points per possession (should be no effect). Multiplicity: single primary hypothesis, no multiple testing beyond falsification. Decision rule: significant if p<0.05 with robust standard errors, otherwise inconclusive. Data version: use complete regular season data up to 2025-26.

But since I'm saying do_not_proceed, I'll mention that the decision is due to low power and high risk of confounding artifacts as shown by prior studies like SF-APPS-041 and SF35, combined with small sample. So I'll set testability p_testable fairly low, maybe 0.3, with blocking constraints like SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, CONFOUNDING, MEASURE_RELIABILITY.

Now, predicted_outcome probabilities: likely uncertain (inconclusive) or untestable. I'd say: supported 0.1, rejected 0.2, untestable 0.2, artifact 0.2, uncertain 0.3 (since power low). Sum 1.0.

historical_effect: changed_decision: no, because the historical evidence didn't alter; but we might have been uncertain before, and the evidence from prior artifacts reinforces the decision not to proceed. But it's not a change; we start from no prior decision, so I'll state "no_historical_evidence" or "no"? Actually, we didn't have a decision before retrieval; so the retrieval informed the decision. The question: "whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision." In stage 1 we didn't make a decision. So I'll put changed_decision: "no", explanation: "No prior decision existed; historical evidence informed the current assessment, highlighting prior artifact risks and the lack of direct evidence on the predictive question, but did not change a pre-existing decision."

But to be precise: I think they expect to know if the retrieval changed a hypothetical decision we might have made without it. I'll set changed_decision: "no", with explanation that it reinforced caution but didn't change from a default of proceed. Could be "no_historical_evidence" if no relevant evidence, but we have some. I'll put "no".

Alright, let's construct the final JSON. Ensure all fields filled. We'll use the risk codes. For blocking constraints in testability, list the main ones. I'll include SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, CONFOUNDING, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, maybe RTM_SELECTION. I'll list them.

Now, careful with the schema: testability.p_testable is a number between 0 and 1. I'll put 0.35. blocking_constraints array of objects with code and text. I'll include: {"code": "SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER", "text": "Only 148 absence spells, many with short durations, limiting power to detect a modest correlation between noisy measures."}, {"code": "CONFOUNDING", "text": "Observed relationship may be driven by opponent defensive strength or simultaneous roster changes; prior studies SF-APPS-041 and SF35 show how such confounds produce artifacts."}, {"code": "MEASURE_RELIABILITY", "text": "Reorganization metric derived from play-type distributions may have low reliability for short spells; PPP changes are inherently noisy."}, {"code": "RTM_SELECTION", "text": "Absences often follow extreme offensive performance; regression to the mean could create spurious correlation between reorganization and PPP change."}

Also, the design: I'll fill as described. Need data_version string, maybe "NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 per-game play-by-play, substitution, and derived play-type possessions".

Now, historical_evidence: I'll list all four, but only FAM:SF-APPS-088 directly relevant. For each, status: FAM:SF-APPS-088 -> "supported", FAM:SF-APPS-078 -> "not a hypothesis test", FAM:SF-APPS-041 -> "artifact", FAM:SF35 -> "artifact". I'll include findings as recorded. Then failed_approaches: from FAM:SF-APPS-041 and FAM:SF35. For FAM:SF-APPS-078 it's not a failure per se, but no hypothesis test, so I'll leave it out. For failed_approaches: FAM:SF-APPS-041: what_failed: "Causal isolation of putback suppression on next possession", why: "Failure to control for game state confounding (score/margin); apparent effect vanished after matching." FAM:SF35: what_failed: "Attributing next-game playing time response to opponent 3P luck", why: "Confounding by game N role; effect disappeared when controlling for game-N share.".

Now, evidence_establishes: "Connector absences cause larger offensive identity breaks (D_A) than usage-matched non-organizer absences, demonstrating that absence type influences reorganization magnitude." Also "Prior studies have identified confounding as a critical risk, with apparent effects failing to survive control for state/role confounds." Evidence_does_not_establish: "Whether the amount of reorganization predicts change in points per possession; no prior study examined this predictive relationship."

own_inferences: "The question is novel; the available absence spells are limited (n~148) and the measures noisy, making a definitive test underpowered. A carefully controlled regression could be attempted but is likely to yield inconclusive results. Any observed correlation may be confounded by opponent strength and other team changes."

I'll indicate that if proceeding, need to collect more seasons to increase sample size, improve measurement reliability by requiring minimum possessions per spell, and use rigorous controls.

design: I'll fill the fields with the planned approach. estimand: "The linear regression slope of change in team offensive rating (points per 100 possessions) on offensive reorganization (divergence of play-type distribution from pre-absence baseline L, computed over the first 5 games of absence) during a player's absence spell." unit: "absence spell". sample: "All absence spells of at least 3 games and with at least 100 offensive possessions in the pre-absence and absence periods, from 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons." power: "Power to detect a correlation of 0.2 is ~0.66 for 148 spells, but after measurement error likely below 0.5; with additional seasons could reach 0.8." controls: "Team and season fixed effects; opponent adjusted offensive rating (rolling 10-game average); home/away indicator; rest days; number of other players missing; pre-absence team offensive rating to account for regression to the mean." falsification: "Test that reorganization does not predict change in defensive rating (points allowed per 100 possessions); null expected." multiplicity: "Single primary hypothesis; no adjustments beyond falsification test." decision_rule: "Reject null if p<0.05 (two-sided) using cluster-robust standard errors by team; otherwise report effect size with confidence interval and declare inconclusive." data_version: "NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 per-game play-by-play and substitution data, with derived play-type possession records, as of 2026-11-01."

Now, testability: p_testable: 0.35. blocking_constraints: list the ones above.

Finally, historical_effect: changed_decision: "no", explanation: "No prior decision; historical evidence from FAM:SF-APPS-088 informed that reorganization metrics exist, while SF-APPS-041 and SF35 highlighted confounding risks, reinforcing the caution to not proceed without addressing low power and confounders.
